interactions.summary: After hearing the case for multicultural openness, Jiang asks why creativity still seems depleted; students answer with comfort, technology, materialism, spiritual distance, and hopelessness, and Jiang concludes Dante would see the present as worse because it no longer produces great art.

speaker_notes.note: The long student answer on spiritual distance is partially truncated by ASR but clearly extends the materialism-and-hopelessness diagnosis.

claims.claim: A student says multiculturalism can expand perspective by forcing debate among values and letting truth be examined from different lenses.
Jiang counters by asking why today's world still appears creatively barren if openness and money are supposed to liberate talent.
Students explain creative decline through comfort, technology, materialism, spiritual disconnection, and loss of love or hope.
Jiang says Dante would look at the present and judge it worse than his own age because even a bad older world could still produce something like the Divine Comedy.

signature_moments.moment: Modern abundance is judged more damning than medieval hardship because it cannot make a Divine Comedy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is a lot worse than my world
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the lecture's civilizational verdict on modernity, not just one more complaint about taste.

chronology_notes.note: The debate turns from immigration toward a broader criterion for social health: whether a civilization can still generate serious art and spiritual energy.

uncertainty_notes.note: The end of Jiang's sentence is truncated by ASR, but the contrast is clear: he is measuring societies by their capacity to produce major creative work.
